1	# Issue #230: a browser page on the remote port, investigation notes
2	
3	Read: CLAUDE.md, docs/lessons.md (84 lines, nothing about the remote port;
4	its lesson is the action/effect core, a fake for every port, and "spike
5	risky technology first"), docs/remote-client.md §§0–5, design.md "Trust
6	boundary" (l.219) and the start of "Remote client (2026-10-12)" (l.3107),
7	plus the code below. Line numbers are as they are in this worktree at
8	7fe8949. There is no `web/` directory yet.
9	
10	## The record first: what is on disk, and how it comes back
11	
12	- **No new record kind and no `model.rs` change is needed.** A browser is
13	  one more `PairedDevice` (`src/ports/remote.rs:96-107`: `id`, `name`,
14	  `scope`, `token_sha256`, `created`, `last_seen`) in
15	  `<data dir>/devices.json`. That file is a bare `Vec<PairedDevice>`
16	  with no schema version (`RemoteFiles::load_devices`/`save_devices`,
17	  `src/adapters/remote.rs:80-86`), written atomically by
18	  `Effect::SaveDevices` (`src/core/remote.rs:121-125`). The name comes
19	  from `/pair`'s `device_name` (`src/app.rs:3650-3655`), cut to 64 chars
20	  in `AppCore::new_device` (`src/core/remote.rs:166-175`). So "Safari on
21	  iPhone" can be the page's own `device_name` with no host change. If
22	  the plan wants a `kind` (browser or native) on the device, it is an
23	  additive `#[serde(default)]` field in a file that has no version.
24	- **Rehydration** is unchanged: `IdentityLoaded { identity, devices,
25	  rotated }` (`src/core/remote.rs:22-30`) puts the devices back at
26	  launch. A token is checked by hash against them on every request
27	  (`authenticate`, `src/app.rs:3125-3153`; `device_by_token`,
28	  `src/core/remote.rs:145-147`). Revoke (`RevokeDevice`,
29	  `src/core/remote.rs:86-92`) and scope change (`:93-100`) apply on the
30	  next request, and revoke closes the device's socket (test
31	  `revoke_closes_the_devices_socket`, `tests/remote.rs:2892`).
32	- **The pairing window is not durable** (`PairingWindow` in core state:
33	  code, scope, `until`, failures; `OpenPairing`/`ClosePairing`/
34	  `PairingFailed`/`Paired`, `src/core/remote.rs:46-73`). The QR is built
35	  in the UI from it (`src/ui/remote.rs:155-173`). Changing JSON to a URL
36	  is a change to that `json!` call and to the "Copy invite" text (`:199-206`),
37	  not to any record.
38	- **The page itself is not a record.** It is static bytes compiled in
39	  (`include_str!`). On the device, what persists is the token, plus
40	  whatever the page keeps to say "identity changed". Decision 2 picks
41	  where that is. The browser also keeps its certificate exception per
42	  host. The host keeps nothing new per browser beyond the device record.
43	- **Identity** (`identity.json`, `Identity` at `src/ports/remote.rs:26-42`,
44	  `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION = 1` at `:17`). It holds the certificate
45	  (base64 DER) and `spki_sha256`. The certificate is made by
46	  `make_identity` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:95-127`) with
47	  `CertificateParams::new(Vec::<String>::new())`: **no subjectAltName at
48	  all**, a CN of `Switchboard <server_id>`, rcgen's default validity
49	  (the comment says `not_after` is the year 4096), and no EKU set
50	  explicitly. The native clients pin the SPKI and ignore names, so this
51	  never mattered. A browser checks names and validity. Changing the
52	  certificate (adding SANs for the LAN address or a `.local` name, or a
53	  bounded validity) changes nothing the pin sees if the key is reused
54	  (the SPKI is the same, §5). But the certificate is stored in
55	  `identity.json`, so reissuing it means writing that file, and an
56	  address that moves would need another reissue.
57	
58	## What the code does today, piece by piece
59	
60	### The listener (`src/adapters/remote.rs`)
61	
62	- `read_request` (`:444-513`) keeps the method, the path, the query
63	  (undecoded), the body, `bearer` (`Authorization: Bearer`, `:487-491`)
64	  and `upgrade` (`Sec-WebSocket-Key` when `Upgrade: websocket`,
65	  `:492-495`). It throws away every other header. **It does not read
66	  `Cookie`, `Origin`, `User-Agent`, `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, `Host`,
67	  `If-None-Match` or `Accept`.** Either token transport in decision 2
68	  needs a new `RemoteRequest` field. That struct is in
69	  `src/adapters/remote.rs:359-372`, which is not under `ports/`, but
70	  `tests/remote.rs` builds requests and should be checked.
71	- `respond` (`:530-552`) always writes `Content-Type: application/json`
72	  and `Connection: keep-alive`, nothing else. It has no CSP, no
73	  Cache-Control, no Set-Cookie and no other content type. `RemoteReply`
74	  (`:388-393`) is `{status, body, authenticated}`. Static files and a
75	  cookie on `/pair` therefore need `RemoteReply` (or a separate
76	  connection-thread path) to carry headers. `respond_upgrade`
77	  (`:519-527`) writes no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`. A browser that offered
78	  a subprotocol fails the handshake if the server does not echo one
79	  (that is a question below, not checked).
80	- Pools and windows: `MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED = 4`, `MAX_PAIRED = 12`
81	  (`:567-568`). A stream past the 4 is dropped at accept (`:699-706`). A
82	  connection moves pools only when a reply says `authenticated: true`
83	  (`:834-849`). `HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT` is 5 s (`:570`), and the first
84	  request line has the same deadline. `IDLE_TIMEOUT` is 30 s (`:573`).
85	  The rate windows exist only for `/api/v1/pair` (6/min) and
86	  `/api/v1/info` (60/min) (`:583-587`, `Limits::limited` `:629-640`).
87	  Any other path, a static one included, is unlimited and goes to the
88	  frame. What this means for a page load: a browser opens several
89	  parallel connections and keeps them alive. Static GETs leave a
90	  connection in the unauthenticated pool for up to 30 s idle. A
91	  failed TLS handshake (the certificate warning) also holds a slot until
92	  it ends. **The pool of 4 is what an unpaired page load competes for.**
93	  Once paired, each fetch with the cookie or token moves its connection
94	  to the paired pool. The test `stalled_strangers_fill_their_own_pool_and_never_a_paired_clients`
95	  (`tests/remote.rs:3226`) is the existing model for that behaviour.
96	- The frame drain: `port.poll(DRAIN_PER_PASS)` then `serve_remote` for
97	  each (`src/app.rs:1585-1597`). The connection thread answers 429/503/504
98	  without the frame (`src/adapters/remote.rs:787-833`). Static bytes
99	  could be answered on the connection thread the same way (they need no
100	  core state), or on the frame through `serve_remote`. §4.1 "the frame
101	  does core state only" leans toward the connection thread. Not decided
102	  here.
103	
104	### The router (`src/app.rs`)
105	
106	- `serve_remote` (`:3017-3121`) refuses any path without the `/api/v1/`
107	  prefix with 404 `not_found` (`:3023-3025`). Then it answers `info` and
108	  `pair` unauthenticated (`:3027-3031`), authenticates, and handles
109	  `events` (`:3036-3038`) and the allowlist. The static paths would be a
110	  new arm before the prefix match, and they are the third thing served
111	  before pairing (§5's rule, `docs/remote-client.md` l.390 in the
112	  section, "Require pairing before anything but `/info` and `/pair`").
113	- `authenticate` (`:3125-3153`) knows only `request.bearer`. Both its
114	  refusals have the code `unauthorized`, with different messages: "pair
115	  this device first" (no token) and "the token is not known; pair again"
116	  (revoked, rotated, or never valid). **A page cannot tell "revoked"
117	  from "never paired" by the code.** With an HttpOnly cookie, the page
118	  cannot even see whether it holds a token. The "revoked" state in the
119	  issue needs either a distinct code (additive) or a non-secret marker
120	  the page keeps itself (for example, "I paired with server X as device
121	  Y").
122	- `remote_subscribe` (`:2723-2758`) requires `request.upgrade` and a
123	  device. It does not check `Origin`. Neither does anything else.
124	- `remote_pair` (`:3606-3674`) compares the body's `spki_sha256` with the
125	  host's own, then the code, uppercased. It counts a failure on either
126	  (`PairingFailed`). It answers `{token, scope, server_id, device_id}` in
127	  the envelope. A cookie would be set here.
128	- `remote_info` (`:3568-3600`) carries `spki_sha256`, `server_name`,
129	  `capabilities`, `version`, `pairing_open`, but not the device's scope
130	  (it is unauthenticated). The header's "scope" comes from the `/pair`
131	  reply, and after that from nowhere: **no endpoint today tells a device
132	  its current scope**. A scope change in the dialog is invisible until a
133	  `control` command is refused. The Swift client has the same gap.
134	- `refuse` (`:3754-3772`) logs method and path, never the query. A
135	  `GET /?code=…` that reached the router would not log the code. Any
136	  new static handler must keep that true.
137	
138	### The session list and the excerpt
139	
140	- `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:636-688`) has `kind`, `card` (the
141	  card's word), `waiting`, `waiting_reason`, `liveness`,
142	  `trust_question`, `prompt_refusal`, `last_stop_at_ms`,
143	  `last_activity_ms`. **It has no excerpt or last-message field.** The
144	  §4.3 text (l.291 of the spec section) calls the card's one-line excerpt
145	  "`last_message` from the `Stop` hook on the record, a field of the
146	  session's metadata". That field is not on the wire, and `grep` finds no
147	  `last_message` in `control/src/lib.rs` or `src/app.rs`. The headset
148	  fills its compact card by fetching `sessions/{id}/last-response` per
149	  session (`client/Sources/SwitchboardUI/BrowserView.swift:149-163`). So
150	  either the page does the same (N requests and N watches, against a
151	  watch set capped at 128), or the issue's "No new read model unless the
152	  page cannot do without one" is tested right here.
153	- Grouped by project: `GET projects` then `GET projects/{id}/sessions`
154	  each, or `GET waiting` for the waiting set. That is what the headset
155	  does. Worker records are hidden unless `?scope=all` (`hide_workers`,
156	  `:3116-3118`).
157	- The session view: `last-response` for a Claude session, `screen`
158	  otherwise. Both are content keys that need `watch` frames on the
159	  socket for `changed` (§4.4 "Watch frames"). The page must speak
160	  `watch`/`unwatch`, wait for `watching`, then fetch.
161	- Reply box: `POST sessions/{id}/send` with `{op, text}` under `control`
162	  (`remote_command`, `:3159`). The page makes the op (needs
163	  `crypto.randomUUID`, which only exists in a secure context; see
164	  questions) and follows §4.5's `/ops/{op}` rule on a timeout.
165	
166	### Pairing UI and the text paths
167	
168	- QR payload: `src/ui/remote.rs:160-166`, a JSON object with
169	  `addresses` holding at most one `ip:port` from `remote::local_address()`
170	  (`src/adapters/remote.rs:962-970`, the outward route's source
171	  address). An IPv6 result would need brackets in a URL. The address is
172	  whatever the route picks, not necessarily the one the phone reaches.
173	- Swift: `PairingInvite.parse` decodes JSON only
174	  (`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:93-116`).
175	  `switchboard-remote pair '<invite json>'` or `pair <host:port> <code>
176	  <spki>` (`client/Sources/switchboard-remote/main.swift:12-13,
177	  107-125`). `PairingInvite` is used by `ConnectionManager.swift`,
178	  `BrowserView.swift` and eight test files under `client/Tests`. Taking a
179	  URL means `parse` tries URL first (`URLComponents`, `code`/`key`/`id`)
180	  and JSON second. `addresses` comes from the URL's host and port.
181	- The README dev-aid text (l.265-278) documents "Copy invite" as the QR
182	  text and `switchboard-remote pair "$(pbpaste)"`. It must change with
183	  the payload.
184	- The script line `pairing <code>` (README l.278, `src/script.rs`) opens
185	  a window with a known code. That is enough to drive the page by hand
186	  against a test data dir.
187	
188	### Tests that exist and what extends
189	
190	- `tests/remote.rs` speaks raw HTTP/1.1 over a pinned rustls client
191	  (`http`, `:245-296`). It reads `Content-Length` only and keeps no other
192	  header, so header assertions (CSP, Cache-Control, Set-Cookie,
193	  Content-Type) need it to return headers. The relevant neighbours are
194	  `info_is_served_to_anyone_and_every_other_read_is_refused_unpaired`
195	  (`:426`), `the_allowlist_refuses_everything_else_with_no_side_effect`
196	  (`:682`), `pair_is_rate_limited_per_listener` (`:1406`),
197	  `subscribe_at` (`:1960`) and `the_client_fixtures_decode_on_both_sides`
198	  (`:1829`, `client/Fixtures`).
199	- "Every path the page references is served" can be a test over the
200	  embedded strings. The page is plain JS with no runner in the tree, so
201	  its logic (query parse, `replaceState`, revision reconcile) is
202	  untested unless the plan adds a JS test harness, which the issue rules
203	  out as a dependency. The page's protocol logic is therefore checked
204	  only by hand.
205	- CI runs on Linux. `include_str!` of `web/*` is portable.
206	
207	## Things the issue asserts that the tree contradicts or leaves open
208	
209	- "Any path outside `/api/v1/` is refused": true (`src/app.rs:3023`), but
210	  on the frame, after the request was queued (so it costs inbox space),
211	  not at the connection thread.
212	- "the one-line excerpt the card shows" is not on the wire (above).
213	- "the device's scope in the header": no endpoint returns it after
214	  pairing (above).
215	- "'revoked' said plainly": the refusal code does not distinguish it
216	  (above).
217	- The `key` check in the page compares the URL's key with what `/info`
218	  says. A page cannot read the TLS certificate it is talking over, so
219	  this proves only that the host *claims* that key. A relay forwards
220	  `/info` faithfully, and the host's own `spki_sha256` check in
221	  `remote_pair` (`:3639-3647`) is fed by the page's body, which is the
222	  impostor's page under a relay. What it does catch is a genuine page on
223	  the wrong genuine host (a second installation at that address or
224	  port, or a rotated key). The issue says roughly this. The tree adds
225	  that §5's sentence "the host refuses a pairing whose `spki_sha256` is
226	  not its own, so a relayed request … fails" does not hold for a
227	  browser, and the spec text must say so.
228	- Cookies are scoped by host, not by port. Two Switchboard instances on
229	  one Mac (`SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT`, design §3.1) and any other HTTPS
230	  service on another port of that host would all receive a
231	  `Secure` cookie set by one of them. A cookie name per `server_id`
232	  avoids the clash between instances. It does not stop another service
233	  on that host from receiving it. `localStorage` is per origin
234	  (scheme, host and port), so it does not have this problem, but any
235	  script on the origin can read it.
236	
237	## Open questions
238	
239	- [owner] Decision 1: is the click-through on the local network the trust step, said in the dialog, or does the host offer its certificate (or a profile) for download to install first?
240	- [source] Does iOS/iPadOS Safari let the owner proceed past a self-signed certificate that has no subjectAltName and only a CN, served on a bare IP? Same question for Chrome, Firefox and macOS Safari.
241	- [source] After a click-through, does each browser (WebKit on iOS especially) apply the per-host exception to `wss://` WebSocket connections and to `fetch` from the page, or only to top-level navigation?
242	- [run] On a real iPhone, does the page load, `fetch` and `new WebSocket` work end to end against the current certificate after the warning is accepted?
243	- [source] Does a page whose certificate was accepted by click-through count as a secure context, so that `crypto.randomUUID`, `Secure` cookies and `SameSite` behave as on a valid HTTPS origin?
244	- [source] If the certificate is to be installed on the device instead: what does iOS require of a manually trusted TLS server certificate (SAN required, EKU `serverAuth`, a maximum validity such as 825 days, the root-trust toggle), and would a year-4096 `not_after` be refused?
245	- [owner] Should the identity's certificate be reissued over the same key with SANs (the LAN IP, a `.local` name) and a bounded validity? Who reissues it when the address changes?
246	- [tree] Can the certificate be reissued over the existing Keychain key without changing `spki_sha256`, through the existing `identity.json` atomic save? (`make_identity` always makes a new key today.)
247	- [source] Does a browser remember the click-through exception across launches, and for how long (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, iOS)? Is the exception lost when the host's IP changes?
248	- [owner] Decision 2: HttpOnly `Secure; SameSite=Strict` cookie, or the token as a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` value with the token in page storage?
249	- [source] Are cookies set with `SameSite=Strict` sent on a same-origin `new WebSocket()` handshake in Safari, Chrome and Firefox? Does `Secure` work for an IP-address host?
250	- [source] With a subprotocol token, must the server echo a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` in the 101 for the browser to accept the connection, and do browsers restrict the characters (base64url) in that value?
251	- [owner] Should the host check `Origin` on the WebSocket upgrade and on POSTs (against cross-site WebSocket hijacking and CSRF), and what exact origin does it accept, given the host can be reached by IP, `.local` name or loopback?
252	- [owner] Cookies are shared across ports on one host: should the cookie name carry the `server_id`, and is a token cookie that other HTTPS services on the same Mac also receive acceptable?
253	- [tree] Does anything in `tests/remote.rs` or `src/app.rs` construct `RemoteRequest` or `RemoteReply` literally, so that adding `cookie`, `origin`, `user_agent` and response-header fields touches them? Is `RemoteRequest` part of the "shared contract" the CLAUDE.md additivity rule covers? (It lives in `adapters/`, not `ports/`.)
254	- [owner] How does the page tell "revoked" from "never paired" from "cookie lost": a new refusal code from `authenticate`, a non-secret marker the page keeps, or both?
255	- [owner] Where does the header's scope come from after pairing: a new authenticated endpoint (for example `GET /api/v1/device` or a field on an authenticated `info`), or the `/pair` reply only, accepting that it goes stale?
256	- [owner] The card excerpt: add an excerpt field to `SessionView` (additive in `control/`, a fixture change on both sides), or have the page fetch `last-response` per listed session as the headset does?
257	- [tree] Does the record carry a `last_message` from the `Stop` hook that could become that field, or is the card's excerpt computed from the transcript cache (`refresh_captions`, `src/app.rs:1093`)?
258	- [run] With the watch set capped at 128 keys, does a page watching `conversation` for every listed Claude session evict the headset's watches on a host with many sessions?
259	- [owner] Decision 3: one QR holding the URL, with the JSON dropped? Is anything left (the visionOS paste field, `BrowserView`, the CLI, fixtures) that needs the JSON form?
260	- [tree] Which Swift call sites and tests under `client/` construct or parse `PairingInvite`, and do any of them depend on `addresses` being a list?
261	- [owner] In the URL, the host part comes from `local_address()`: the IP, a `.local` hostname, or both (two QRs)? What should happen when the route-chosen address is not the one the phone can reach?
262	- [source] When a phone's camera opens the URL and the certificate interstitial shows first, is the URL with the code recorded in browser history, the tab list or iCloud tab sync before the page's `replaceState` can run?
263	- [source] Does `history.replaceState` remove the query from Safari's history entry and from "recently closed" on iOS, or only from the address bar?
264	- [owner] Decision 4: the exact static paths (`/`, `/app.js`, `/app.css`, a favicon?) and their Content-Type and CSP. Should static bytes be answered on the connection thread or the frame, and with which cache policy (no-store, or an ETag from `version`)?
265	- [owner] Should static paths get a rate window of their own, and do they count against the unauthenticated pool of 4 as today?
266	- [run] Does a normal page load (parallel connections, keep-alive, `/favicon.ico`, the failed handshake behind the warning) exhaust the pool of 4 and get connections dropped at accept on iOS Safari?
267	- [source] How many parallel HTTP/1.1 connections per host does iOS Safari open, and how long does it keep an idle one?
268	- [owner] Does the static-path arm amend §5's "before pairing" rule in the spec and the design.md remote status section, and in what words?
269	- [owner] What does the page show when opened with neither a code nor a token: "open the pairing window and scan", a code-entry form, or both?
270	- [owner] Decision 6: should the device record gain an additive `kind` (browser or native) or a user-agent field, or is the name enough?
271	- [owner] Should the page be HTML, CSS and JS under `web/` served by `include_str!` with no JS test harness, which leaves the page's reconcile logic untested by CI?
272	- [run] Is the end-to-end pairing flow over the host's own HTTP client (as `tests/remote.rs` does) enough for acceptance, or does the owner need a manual phone run recorded?
273	- [owner] On the page, a reply to a session sitting at the folder-trust question, `prompt_refusal`, and resume: in scope for the first cut, or hidden?
274	- [source] Does the Bonjour `.local` name resolve from iOS Safari, and would it be a better URL host than the IP?
275	
276	What I did not check: no browser behaviour, iOS rule or crate API was looked up, and nothing was run. I did not read `src/script.rs`, the Swift `ConnectionManager`, `client/Fixtures`, design.md past the first part of the remote status section, or spike 22's README. The `last_message` grep covered only `control/src/lib.rs`, `src/app.rs` and the Swift protocol files.

  address that moves would need another reissue.

## What the code does today, piece by piece

### The listener (`src/adapters/remote.rs`)

- `read_request` (`:444-513`) keeps the method, the path, the query
  (undecoded), the body, `bearer` (`Authorization: Bearer`, `:487-491`)
  and `upgrade` (`Sec-WebSocket-Key` when `Upgrade: websocket`,
  `:492-495`). It throws away every other header. **It does not read
  `Cookie`, `Origin`, `User-Agent`, `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, `Host`,
  `If-None-Match` or `Accept`.** Either token transport in decision 2
  needs a new `RemoteRequest` field. That struct is in
  `src/adapters/remote.rs:359-372`, which is not under `ports/`, but
  `tests/remote.rs` builds requests and should be checked.
- `respond` (`:530-552`) always writes `Content-Type: application/json`
  and `Connection: keep-alive`, nothing else. It has no CSP, no
  Cache-Control, no Set-Cookie and no other content type. `RemoteReply`
  (`:388-393`) is `{status, body, authenticated}`. Static files and a
  cookie on `/pair` therefore need `RemoteReply` (or a separate
  connection-thread path) to carry headers. `respond_upgrade`
  (`:519-527`) writes no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`. A browser that offered
  a subprotocol fails the handshake if the server does not echo one
  (that is a question below, not checked).
- Pools and windows: `MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED = 4`, `MAX_PAIRED = 12`
  (`:567-568`). A stream past the 4 is dropped at accept (`:699-706`). A
  connection moves pools only when a reply says `authenticated: true`
  (`:834-849`). `HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT` is 5 s (`:570`), and the first
  request line has the same deadline. `IDLE_TIMEOUT` is 30 s (`:573`).
  The rate windows exist only for `/api/v1/pair` (6/min) and
  `/api/v1/info` (60/min) (`:583-587`, `Limits::limited` `:629-640`).
  Any other path, a static one included, is unlimited and goes to the
  frame. What this means for a page load: a browser opens several
  parallel connections and keeps them alive. Static GETs leave a
  connection in the unauthenticated pool for up to 30 s idle. A
  failed TLS handshake (the certificate warning) also holds a slot until
  it ends. **The pool of 4 is what an unpaired page load competes for.**
  Once paired, each fetch with the cookie or token moves its connection
  to the paired pool. The test `stalled_strangers_fill_their_own_pool_and_never_a_paired_clients`
  (`tests/remote.rs:3226`) is the existing model for that behaviour.
- The frame drain: `port.poll(DRAIN_PER_PASS)` then `serve_remote` for
  each (`src/app.rs:1585-1597`). The connection thread answers 429/503/504
  without the frame (`src/adapters/remote.rs:787-833`). Static bytes
  could be answered on the connection thread the same way (they need no
  core state), or on the frame through `serve_remote`. §4.1 "the frame
  does core state only" leans toward the connection thread. Not decided
  here.

### The router (`src/app.rs`)

- `serve_remote` (`:3017-3121`) refuses any path without the `/api/v1/`
  prefix with 404 `not_found` (`:3023-3025`). Then it answers `info` and
  `pair` unauthenticated (`:3027-3031`), authenticates, and handles
  `events` (`:3036-3038`) and the allowlist. The static paths would be a
  new arm before the prefix match, and they are the third thing served
  before pairing (§5's rule, `docs/remote-client.md` l.390 in the
  section, "Require pairing before anything but `/info` and `/pair`").
- `authenticate` (`:3125-3153`) knows only `request.bearer`. Both its
  refusals have the code `unauthorized`, with different messages: "pair
  this device first" (no token) and "the token is not known; pair again"
  (revoked, rotated, or never valid). **A page cannot tell "revoked"
  from "never paired" by the code.** With an HttpOnly cookie, the page
  cannot even see whether it holds a token. The "revoked" state in the
  issue needs either a distinct code (additive) or a non-secret marker
  the page keeps itself (for example, "I paired with server X as device
  Y").
- `remote_subscribe` (`:2723-2758`) requires `request.upgrade` and a
  device. It does not check `Origin`. Neither does anything else.
- `remote_pair` (`:3606-3674`) compares the body's `spki_sha256` with the
  host's own, then the code, uppercased. It counts a failure on either
  (`PairingFailed`). It answers `{token, scope, server_id, device_id}` in
  the envelope. A cookie would be set here.
- `remote_info` (`:3568-3600`) carries `spki_sha256`, `server_name`,
  `capabilities`, `version`, `pairing_open`, but not the device's scope
  (it is unauthenticated). The header's "scope" comes from the `/pair`
  reply, and after that from nowhere: **no endpoint today tells a device
  its current scope**. A scope change in the dialog is invisible until a
  `control` command is refused. The Swift client has the same gap.
- `refuse` (`:3754-3772`) logs method and path, never the query. A
  `GET /?code=…` that reached the router would not log the code. Any
  new static handler must keep that true.

### The session list and the excerpt

- `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:636-688`) has `kind`, `card` (the
  card's word), `waiting`, `waiting_reason`, `liveness`,
  `trust_question`, `prompt_refusal`, `last_stop_at_ms`,
  `last_activity_ms`. **It has no excerpt or last-message field.** The
  §4.3 text (l.291 of the spec section) calls the card's one-line excerpt
  "`last_message` from the `Stop` hook on the record, a field of the
  session's metadata". That field is not on the wire, and `grep` finds no
  `last_message` in `control/src/lib.rs` or `src/app.rs`. The headset
  fills its compact card by fetching `sessions/{id}/last-response` per
  session (`client/Sources/SwitchboardUI/BrowserView.swift:149-163`). So
  either the page does the same (N requests and N watches, against a
  watch set capped at 128), or the issue's "No new read model unless the
  page cannot do without one" is tested right here.
- Grouped by project: `GET projects` then `GET projects/{id}/sessions`
  each, or `GET waiting` for the waiting set. That is what the headset
  does. Worker records are hidden unless `?scope=all` (`hide_workers`,
  `:3116-3118`).
- The session view: `last-response` for a Claude session, `screen`
  otherwise. Both are content keys that need `watch` frames on the
  socket for `changed` (§4.4 "Watch frames"). The page must speak
  `watch`/`unwatch`, wait for `watching`, then fetch.
- Reply box: `POST sessions/{id}/send` with `{op, text}` under `control`
  (`remote_command`, `:3159`). The page makes the op (needs
  `crypto.randomUUID`, which only exists in a secure context; see
  questions) and follows §4.5's `/ops/{op}` rule on a timeout.

- `tests/remote.rs` speaks raw HTTP/1.1 over a pinned rustls client

  header, so header assertions (CSP, Cache-Control, Set-Cookie,

## Things the issue asserts that the tree contradicts or leaves open

- "Any path outside `/api/v1/` is refused": true (`src/app.rs:3023`), but
  on the frame, after the request was queued (so it costs inbox space),
  not at the connection thread.
- "the one-line excerpt the card shows" is not on the wire (above).
- "the device's scope in the header": no endpoint returns it after
  pairing (above).
- "'revoked' said plainly": the refusal code does not distinguish it
  (above).
- The `key` check in the page compares the URL's key with what `/info`
  says. A page cannot read the TLS certificate it is talking over, so
  this proves only that the host *claims* that key. A relay forwards
  `/info` faithfully, and the host's own `spki_sha256` check in
  `remote_pair` (`:3639-3647`) is fed by the page's body, which is the
  impostor's page under a relay. What it does catch is a genuine page on
  the wrong genuine host (a second installation at that address or
  port, or a rotated key). The issue says roughly this. The tree adds
  that §5's sentence "the host refuses a pairing whose `spki_sha256` is
  not its own, so a relayed request … fails" does not hold for a
  browser, and the spec text must say so.
- Cookies are scoped by host, not by port. Two Switchboard instances on
  one Mac (`SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT`, design §3.1) and any other HTTPS
  service on another port of that host would all receive a
  `Secure` cookie set by one of them. A cookie name per `server_id`
  avoids the clash between instances. It does not stop another service
  on that host from receiving it. `localStorage` is per origin
  (scheme, host and port), so it does not have this problem, but any
  script on the origin can read it.

# Facts for issue #230 (browser page on the remote port)

No spike run; worktree left clean. "W" = WebSearch, "F" = WebFetch. Query text is given per claim.

## Settled

- iOS 13+ TLS server certificates need the DNS name in subjectAltName (CN ignored), `serverAuth` EKU, and validity of 825 days or less. The page makes no exemption for user-trusted certificates. Evidence: https://support.apple.com/103769 (F). Query: W "iOS 13 requirements for TLS server certificates subjectAltName 825 days manually trusted certificate".
- On iOS, a click-through does not carry `wss://`. WebKit bug 41419 is open (NEW, modified 2026-01-12); its 2010 report and a 2011 list thread agree that trusting the certificate made `wss` work and the HTTPS acceptance did not; the maintainer prefers logging to a warning sheet. Evidence: https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=41419 (F); https://lists.webkit.org/pipermail/webkit-dev/2011-June/017385.html (W). Query: W "WebKit Safari iOS WebSocket wss self-signed certificate exception not applied bug". Agreeing project doc: code-server's iPad guide says Safari blocks WebSockets unless the certificate is installed as a profile, with a matching SAN and `CA:true`, and asks for a domain name rather than an IP: https://github.com/cdr/code-server/blob/v3.7.0/doc/ipad.md (F). Query: W "iOS Safari self-signed certificate warning proceed IP address no subjectAltName wss WebSocket". Two sources agree, so the plan must not rely on a click-through for the socket on iOS.
- `.local` names over mDNS reach Mobile Safari on the same network; unicast `.local` DNS is unreliable. Evidence: code-server guide (above, which suggests a `.local` name); https://discussions.apple.com/thread/6555023 (W). Query: W "Safari iOS mDNS .local hostname resolve Bonjour name from Safari". Not tested on a device.
- Chrome 58+ ignores CN and needs the SAN for hostname matching. Evidence: https://textslashplain.com/2017/03/10/chrome-deprecates-subject-cn-matching/ (W, one Chromium engineer's post: a lead). Query: W "Chrome 58 deprecate common name certificate hostname matching subjectAltName only announcement". Safari agrees: https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=158345 (W). The plan builds the SAN regardless.
- A WebSocket that requests a subprotocol must get one back. WHATWG step 11.2 fails the connection if the client sent protocols and the response has no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`; RFC 6455 §4.1 fails it if the server names one the client did not send. Evidence: https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/ (F); https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455.html (F). Query: W "WebSocket Sec-WebSocket-Protocol browser token subprotocol authentication cookie vs protocol header Safari Chrome" (search gave only lead posts; the standards settle it). The server echoes the token protocol in the 101.
- A base64url token is a legal subprotocol value: RFC 7230 `tchar` includes `-` and `_`, and RFC 6455 §4.2.2 takes the value as a `token`, which may not be empty. Evidence: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7230#section-3.2.6 (F); RFC 6455 §4.2.2 (F). Standards query only.
- The server must validate `Origin` on WebSocket upgrades. RFC 6455 §1.3 says Origin protects against unauthorized cross-origin use; §4.2.2 says a server that does not validate it accepts connections from anywhere. Evidence: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455.html (F). The fetch covered the first 100,000 characters only; §10.2 was not read.
- Cookies do not isolate by port (RFC 6265 §8.5), so every HTTPS port on one host receives the same cookies; a `Secure` cookie is sent only on secure schemes (§5.4). Evidence: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6265.html (F). Standards query only.
- For an https origin, `isSecureContext` depends only on the scheme, not on certificate validity: W3C §3.1 step 3 reads "If origin's scheme is either "https" or "wss", return "Potentially Trustworthy"". Evidence: https://www.w3.org/TR/secure-contexts/ (F). Query: W "W3C secure contexts potentially trustworthy origin https certificate error user bypass". What browsers do after a click-through is Unresolved 2.
- `crypto.randomUUID` is secure-context only; `getRandomValues` is not. Evidence: MDN via mirror, https://ligm.univ-eiffel.fr/~forax/MDN/developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Crypto/randomUUID.html (W). Query: W "MDN crypto.randomUUID secure context only available". Generate op ids with `getRandomValues`.
- A `SameSite=Strict` cookie can be missing from a WebSocket in a restored Safari tab. WebKit 200345 (open, last comment 2021-07-08): a Strict cookie is sent on a normal load but only the Lax cookie after "Reopen Last Closed Window". WebKit 232666 (Safari 14/15, RESOLVED CONFIGURATION CHANGED, 2021-11-03): Strict cookies are omitted on WebSockets in restored and history-loaded tabs; the maintainer declined to change old versions. Evidence: https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=200345 (F); https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=232666 (F). Query: W "Safari SameSite=Strict cookie WebSocket handshake sent same-site WebKit". The socket must not depend on a Strict cookie alone.
- The Stop hook's `last_message` is not on the record. `src/adapters/hooks.rs:196` builds `EventKind::Stopped { last_message, pending }`, `src/ports/events.rs:24` carries it, and the core reads only `pending` (`src/core/events.rs:132`). `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs`) has no excerpt field. Tree.
- `WATCH_CAP` is 128 (`src/content.rs:42`). Tree.
- No test under `tests/` builds `RemoteRequest` or `RemoteReply` as a literal. They are built in `src/adapters/remote.rs:506` and `src/app.rs` (`:1664`, `:1679`, `:2365`, `:2371`, `:2376`). Tree.
- `PairingInvite` is used in 12 Swift files: four under `client/Sources` (`switchboard-remote/main.swift`, `SwitchboardUI/BrowserView.swift`, `SwitchboardClientCore/ConnectionManager.swift`, `SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift`) and eight under `client/Tests`. Tree.

## Unresolved

1. Does iOS Safari offer a click-through for an untrusted self-signed certificate on a bare IP? Kurento says iOS "will outright reject untrusted self-signed certs, instead of showing a security warning" (https://doc-kurento.readthedocs.io/en/stable/knowledge/selfsigned_certs.html, F). A search result describes a "Show Details / Visit this website" path, from a third-party manual rather than Apple (W "iPhone Safari 'This Connection Is Not Private' visit this website self-signed certificate local network iOS 17 Show Details"). Sources conflict and the iOS version is unknown. Build to: no dependency on the click-through. Owner: O1.
2. Click-through on Chrome and Firefox for a no-SAN certificate on an IP, and whether `isSecureContext` is `true` after one. Query: W "window.isSecureContext after proceeding past certificate error interstitial Chrome secure context". Only a 2017 secondhand W3C-list report says yes. Build to: SAN in the certificate, and a `getRandomValues` fallback. Owner: O2.
3. Does a click-through persist across launches? Query: W "Chrome certificate exception proceed anyway persist across browser restart session only self-signed". Chrome: no source. Firefox: a Mozilla bug shows "Permanently store this exception" checked by default (a lead). Build to: treat the exception as lost at each launch.
4. Do Chrome and Firefox send `SameSite=Strict` cookies on same-origin WebSocket handshakes? Only WebKit sources found (Settled above). Build to: the token travels in `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, so the socket does not depend on this.
5. Does `Secure` work on an IP-address host in browsers? RFC 6265 §5.4 allows it for a secure scheme; no browser source found. One unanswered Apple Developer Forums post reports a Safari non-resend of an HttpOnly+Secure+SameSite=Strict cookie set on a 101: https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/104488 (F). Build to: the cookie name carries `server_id`, and nothing depends on the cookie for the socket.
6. Connections per host from iOS Safari. Query: W "Chrome max connections per host HTTP/1.1 six parallel connections Safari WebKit per-host limit". Chrome's 6 comes from secondary sources. The WebKit Mac scheduler source returned 404 to F (https://opensource.apple.com/source/WebKit2/WebKit2-7537.71/NetworkProcess/mac/NetworkResourceLoadSchedulerMac.mm.auto.html). Build to: a small page connection count, and measure (O5).
7. rcgen 0.14 defaults. Query: W "rcgen CertificateParams default not_after 4096 self_signed KeyPair from_pem rcgen 0.14"; F https://docs.rs/rcgen/0.14.10/rcgen/struct.CertificateParams.html. The docs give no defaults, and the crate source could not be read from this session. The tree's "year 4096" comment (`src/adapters/remote.rs:91`) is unverified. Build to: set `not_before`, `not_after` (≤825 days), SANs, `serverAuth` EKU and `is_ca` explicitly. Whether `KeyPair::from_pem` exists for a reissue over the stored key is also unverified; compile it before relying on it.
8. Does `history.replaceState` remove the query from Safari's history menu, "recently closed", or iCloud tab sync, or does the browser record the URL before the script runs (including Chrome and Firefox)? Query: W "history.replaceState URL query removed from Safari history recently closed tabs iCloud tab sync before script runs". Nothing on these. One WebKit report says `replaceState` may add history-menu entries, and a maintainer replied that Safari decides what the menu shows (https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=58072, W). Build to: the code is single-use, refused after its first attempt, and expires with the window (five minutes); a leaked URL then grants nothing.

## For the owner

- O1 (Decision 1): On an iPhone, does Safari offer a click-through for the host's certificate on its IP, and does the page then load and fetch? Does a profile with a SAN certificate (CA:true, serverAuth, ≤825 days, full trust enabled) let `wss://` connect? - O3 (Decision 2): On the device, does a token in `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` survive reopening Safari and history navigation? The protocol route does not depend on cookies, so it works either way.
- O4 (Decisions 1 and 3): Does the browser keep the pairing URL in history or tab sync after `replaceState`? Either answer is covered by the single-use code and five-minute expiry in Unresolved 8.
- O5 (Decision 4): How many connections does iOS Safari open to one host on a page load, and how long does it keep them? Measure before the pool size is fixed.

### 4.1 Implementation

- **No Tokio.** The host is std threads and `mpsc`; the core is owned by `SwitchboardApp` and every state change is a dispatch on the frame thread. The remote port follows the `ControlSocket` shape: an accept thread per listener, one thread per connection, each request handed over a channel to the frame, answered by the same `serve` path in `app.rs` (`serve_pending` runs before every frame, hidden ones included), the reply sent back on the connection's channel. A second runtime inside an egui app buys nothing for a handful of connections.
- **The frame does core state only.** A metadata request (a view, a command) is answered on the frame as the control port is. A content request (conversation, screen, run output, file) takes two steps: the frame answers with the **handle and the redaction policy** (the transcript path and resume handle, the pane's host id, the run's log path, the file's root and relative path, plus the secret values to mask and the policy fingerprint), and one **content worker thread** does the read, the parse, the mask, the version check and the serialization from a queue of such requests (one at a time, so one large parse is in memory at once; Spike 22 measured 575 MB peak for the largest transcript), then sends one small action back to the frame to record the version it observed (§4.4), and the connection thread writes the reply. The watch poll (§4.4) runs through the same worker. A multi-megabyte transcript, a 768 KiB file or a slow Keychain call therefore costs the worker its time and the asking connection its wait, never a frame. The handle is read under the frame's authority, so a record removed or rebound between the two steps makes the worker's version action a no-op and the reply carries the handle it read from.
- **Bounds.** The port is one user's few devices, and the limits say so:
  - at most 16 connections in total and 4 unauthenticated ones; a further accept is closed at once. The 4 are a separate pool: an unauthenticated flood fills its own slots and never a paired client's;
  - `/pair` is answered at most six times a minute per listener and `/info` sixty; past that the connection thread answers 429 without reaching the frame;
  - a TLS handshake and the first request line each within 5 s, a request body within 10 s, a write within 10 s; a connection that misses a deadline is closed;
  - one request in flight per connection (HTTP/1.1, no pipelining);
  - the frame drains at most 8 remote requests per pass, in arrival order, the rest waiting on the channel; the channel is bounded at 64 and a full channel answers 503 from the connection thread without reaching the frame; a frame-side request is a view or a handle lookup and takes microseconds, so the count is the bound;
  - each WebSocket subscriber has an event queue of 256; when it fills, the subscriber is sent `resync_required` and closed, never silently trimmed (§4.4);
  - the watch set (§4.4) is capped at 128 keys for the whole port; past the cap the least recently read key is evicted silently, since a read of an evicted key always works and re-enters it.
- Preferred crates: a blocking HTTP/1.1 server over `std::net::TcpListener` (hand-rolled or `tiny_http`), `tungstenite` for WebSocket, `rustls` with `rcgen` for the per-installation certificate, and `mdns-sd` (or the system `dns-sd` through a small macOS adapter) for Bonjour. All of it in `src/adapters/remote.rs` behind a `ports::remote` trait with a fake, and all of it must compile on Linux CI (Bonjour may be a `cfg(target_os = "macos")` adapter with a no-op elsewhere). **Spike 22 (§10) decides the exact crates before any of this is built.**
- Handlers are thin: HTTP request → auth and scope check → allowlist → `wire::Request` → `serve` → redaction → `wire::Reply` → HTTP response. No session or transcript logic lives in the adapter.
- Only the instance holding the store lock listens (as the control port does); a read-only instance refuses to bind.
- Bind to loopback by default until remote access is explicitly enabled in Settings. For LAN access, bind the chosen interface and require pairing.
- Configurable port in `identity.json` (§3.1), default `43187`, overridable with `SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT` (a dev aid, documented in the README) so two instances can run on one machine; `0` picks a free one, which the tests use.
- Advertise `_switchboard._tcp` via Bonjour only while listening on a non-loopback interface. TXT records carry the protocol major version (`v`), the display name (`name`) and the `server_id` (`id`, so a client matches a record to a known server before it connects); never a token, never key material. The instance name is the display name with a short id suffix, so two installations on one machine stay distinct.
- If Switchboard closes, the port goes away. A standalone daemon is not in scope.

### 4.2 API conventions
### 4.4 WebSocket events

Envelope:

```json
{
  "server_id": "uuid",
  "epoch": "uuid",
  "revision": 1042,
  "type": "changed",
  "resource": {"kind": "session", "id": "record-uuid"},
  "at_ms": 1760220000000
}
```

Event types:

- `hello {epoch, revision}`: the first frame on every subscription.
- **Scope.** A listing leaves out the records Dispatch made for its own use: a ticket's project with everything in it, and a worker session (the planner, an implementer, a reviewer) in any project, told by the `<ticket>-<nonce>` form of the op they were made under (`switchboard_control::is_dispatch_worker_op`). A supervisor's records (`sup-…`) and the owner's own are listed as ever, and a worker record is still read by its id, which is how the ticket view to come will reach them. `?scope=all` on `projects`, `sessions`, `waiting` and on the `events` subscription lists them and announces them; a plain subscription gets no `project`, `sessions`, `session` or `runs` frame about one. `info` lists `scope` among its capabilities. The point is the wire: hundreds of worker sessions on a host, which the headset fetched one project at a time, are now neither fetched nor announced.
- `changed {kind, id}` with the **metadata kinds** `project`, `space`, `set`, `session`; the **content kinds** `conversation`, `screen`, `run_output` (`id` = `record/n`), `file` (a pinned file, `id` = `project_id/path`); and the collection kinds `projects`, `spaces`, `sets` (with the space's id), `sessions` (with the project's id), `runs` (with the record's id), `waiting`, emitted when a collection's member id set moves and answered by refetching the collection whole; a global collection's `id` is the empty string. Each kind is its own resource key on the client (§4.2); a member fetched as part of its collection holds the collection's revision until it is read alone.
- `removed {kind, id}`: the resource is gone; the client drops it and marks any window on it "removed on <server>".
- `watching {kind, id}`: the answer to a `watch` frame (below).
- `resync_required`: sent before the host closes a subscriber whose queue overflowed; the client reconnects and refetches everything.

**What produces events.** The host has no event bus, and a save is not a reliable sign of a visible change: working sets save through `SaveViews`, Claude Code's trust question (`PromptSeen`) and a Codex pane going quiet (`HostListed`) change what a card says with no save at all. So the port does not watch for saves. Revision and events come from three places in `app.rs`:

1. **The read-model diff, after every pass.** After every `dispatch` and after every polling pass (`HostListed`, the hook log, `Tick`), the app recomputes a cheap per-resource fingerprint of each exported metadata read model (`SessionView`, `SetView` with its members, `ProjectView`, `SpaceView`, `waiting`) and compares it with the previous pass's. One `changed` per resource whose fingerprint moved, one `removed` per resource that vanished, one `changed` per collection whose membership moved, and `revision` bumped once per pass that emitted anything. The diff is the gate, not the effect list, so a set rename, a pin edit, a trust-question transition, a quiet-state transition and a time-based rule-set change all surface without anyone naming them. The fingerprint is a hash over the view's serialized bytes **with its time-derived fields held at zero**: `quiet_secs` is computed from the clock in `session_view` and would move every pass, so the view gains an additive `last_activity_ms` the client derives quiet from, and the quiet **state** (the card's word moving to idle) is what the diff sees. Collections carry the membership revision of §4.2, bumped only when the member id set moves. The hash is cheap at this scale (hundreds of records); the spike measures it (§10).
2. **Content versions, assigned where content is read.** Conversation text, pane text, run output and pinned files are mutable outside the core and can change between two reads inside one poll interval, so a content reply's revision cannot come from the counter alone. Every content read goes through a per-key **content cache** in `SwitchboardApp`, whose bookkeeping lives on the frame and whose reads run on the connection or worker thread (§4.1). The cache holds, per key, the **source version** and the **policy fingerprint of the owning project (§4.3)** it last served, with the revision it was assigned.    - **transcript**: size and mtime. Claude Code's JSONL only appends, Switchboard never edits one, and `/clear` or a discard rebinds the record to another file, so a growing size is a reliable version and a same-size rewrite does not occur;

- `file.read`: content of a file **only if some working set pins it** (`PinTarget::File` with that project and path). The read goes through a new `ports::files` method, `read_pinned(root, relative)`, not through the UI's preview loader. Confinement is by descriptors, not by path strings, so it stays valid while names change under it:
  - the relative path is rejected if it is absolute, empty, or has a `..` or `.` component, before anything touches the disk (a persisted pin can hold anything);
  - the project root is opened once as a directory descriptor (`O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_CLOEXEC`) and the walk proceeds **one component at a time** with `openat` from the previous descriptor: every directory component with `O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK | O_CLOEXEC`, the last with `O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK | O_CLOEXEC`. A component that is a symlink fails the open (`ELOOP`), so **no symlink anywhere in the path is followed, parent or leaf**; a swap of any directory for a link between two hops is refused at the next hop, and a swap after the hop cannot move the descriptor already held. `openat` comes through a safe wrapper crate (`rustix`; or `cap-std`, which does this walk itself, if the spike prefers it); the crate-wide `unsafe` ban stands;
  - `O_NONBLOCK` on the open is what keeps a FIFO from parking the connection thread for good: the open returns at once, `fstat` on the descriptor must say regular file, and anything else (a FIFO, a socket, a device, a directory as the leaf) is refused before any read. The flag is cleared on the regular file before reading. The read runs on the content worker (§4.1), so even a stall here costs the worker its time, never a frame;
  - the read is `take(limit + 1)` with the port's limit of 768 KiB (§4.2), so growth after the check cannot exceed the limit;
  - dotenv names (`.env`, `.env.*`) are refused whatever is pinned, since those hold the project's secrets;
  - the reply carries the file's `modified` and `size` from the same descriptor, and the content is masked like every other text.
  Both platforms the crate builds on are Unix, so one implementation serves macOS and Linux CI.

If the secret set cannot be resolved (a Keychain error, a missing set), the reply is **refused** with that reason, never sent unredacted and never served from a cached success. What this covers is exactly the values Switchboard holds: a secret the user pasted into a prompt, or one a tool printed that Switchboard never knew, is not found. The paired-devices dialog says this in a sentence, and the claim in design.md's trust boundary is widened to "or as redacted text on the remote port".

New read models, added to the wire crate:

- `session.conversation`: the `Conversation` from `ports::transcript` as a wire shape: title, model, branch, usage, and turns paged by **turn number** (`n`, 1-based). The host parses the whole JSONL, as the session view does, from the app-level cache (§4.4); a transcript the app can show is one the port can serve, and the supported size is whatever the app handles, which the spike measures. What paging bounds is the **response**: a page anchored at its start (`from=turn`) stops at `limit` turns or at the body cap, whichever first, and says `next` for the turn to continue from; a page anchored at its end (`from=last`, or `before=turn` for the page ending before a turn the client holds) fills backward from the anchor, so it always reaches it and `from` is wherever it filled up. The client opens on the tail and walks back with `before`, so a transcript whose turns are large never shows a stale end or a gap; a change is followed from the last turn held page after page until `next` is empty, up to ten pages. A page carries only the first 512 bytes of each tool call's input and result and of each activity's text, marked `more`, which is what keeps a turn with a hundred tool calls to tens of kilobytes rather than hundreds; `session.turn` reads one turn whole, at the conversation's revision, and the client asks for it when a turn's activity is opened. A single turn larger than 256 KiB is cut (final text kept whole where possible, activity text trimmed) and marked `truncated`. The page carries the `resume_id` it was read from: `/clear` and a discard rebind the record to a new transcript, and a client holding turn numbers from another handle drops them and refetches from 1. The last turn is always in progress until a `Stop` event: on a `changed {conversation}` the client refetches from the last turn it holds and **replaces** that turn and everything after it. A handle rebind (`resume_id` moved on the session view) changes the conversation cache's key, which emits `changed {conversation}` of its own, so the client needs no rule linking the two. Only Claude Code sessions have a conversation; Codex, shell, command and service sessions answer with a "no conversation" reason and the client falls back to `screen` (and, for commands and services, `run_output`).
- `session.last_response`: the last turn's `final_text`, its `n` and `end`. It is a **projection of the `conversation` key**: it is read from the same cache, carries the conversation's content revision, is watched by watching `conversation`, and refreshes on `changed {conversation}`; a window showing only the last response registers that watch. The compact card's one-line excerpt is not part of it: that is `last_message` from the `Stop` hook on the record, a field of the session's metadata, and moves with `changed {session}`.
- `session.runs`: a command's or service's runs as the record holds them (`Run`: `n`, started, ended, exit, artifacts' names, not their paths). `session.run_output`: the tail of one run's scrollback log (`scrollback::tail_text`, escapes stripped, `lines` clamped to 500), redacted; a run whose log was pruned or rotated answers with that reason. This is how an exited command whose pane is gone is still readable: `session.screen` refuses a session that is not running, by design.
- `file.read`: content of a file **only if some working set pins it** (`PinTarget::File` with that project and path). The read goes through a new `ports::files` method, `read_pinned(root, relative)`, not through the UI's preview loader. Confinement is by descriptors, not by path strings, so it stays valid while names change under it:
  - the relative path is rejected if it is absolute, empty, or has a `..` or `.` component, before anything touches the disk (a persisted pin can hold anything);
  - the project root is opened once as a directory descriptor (`O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_CLOEXEC`) and the walk proceeds **one component at a time** with `openat` from the previous descriptor: every directory component with `O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK | O_CLOEXEC`, the last with `O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK | O_CLOEXEC`. A component that is a symlink fails the open (`ELOOP`), so **no symlink anywhere in the path is followed, parent or leaf**; a swap of any directory for a link between two hops is refused at the next hop, and a swap after the hop cannot move the descriptor already held. `openat` comes through a safe wrapper crate (`rustix`; or `cap-std`, which does this walk itself, if the spike prefers it); the crate-wide `unsafe` ban stands;
  - `O_NONBLOCK` on the open is what keeps a FIFO from parking the connection thread for good: the open returns at once, `fstat` on the descriptor must say regular file, and anything else (a FIFO, a socket, a device, a directory as the leaf) is refused before any read. The flag is cleared on the regular file before reading. The read runs on the content worker (§4.1), so even a stall here costs the worker its time, never a frame;
  - the read is `take(limit + 1)` with the port's limit of 768 KiB (§4.2), so growth after the check cannot exceed the limit;
  - dotenv names (`.env`, `.env.*`) are refused whatever is pinned, since those hold the project's secrets;
  - the reply carries the file's `modified` and `size` from the same descriptor, and the content is masked like every other text.
  Both platforms the crate builds on are Unix, so one implementation serves macOS and Linux CI.
- `info`: `server_id`, `server_name`, protocol version, capabilities, `epoch`, `revision`, the certificate's public-key hash (SPKI, SHA-256), the port's limits (file limit, conversation page size, body cap), and whether the pairing window is open.

Avoid a general-purpose filesystem endpoint. Paths are never accepted from the client except as the identity of an existing pin.

# Plan: issue #230, a browser page on the remote port

One commit. The app runs at every step: the page is additive, the native
clients keep working through every step, and the last step is the docs.
References are to this worktree at 7fe8949. "Facts" is the facts file.

## Where this departs from the issue

- **"The one-line excerpt the card shows."** There is none on the wire.
  `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:636-688`) has the card word and
  `waiting_reason` and no excerpt, and the Stop hook's `last_message`
  never reaches the record: `src/adapters/hooks.rs:196` builds it,
  `src/core/events.rs:132` reads only `pending` (Facts, Settled). The spec's
  claim that the excerpt is "a field of the session's metadata"
  (`docs/remote-client.md` §4.3, `session.last_response`) is wrong today.
  The page's rows show kind, the card word and `waiting_reason`. For the
  waiting sessions only, at most 8, it also fetches `last-response` once,
  without a `watch`, and shows its first line. The list works without that
  fetch; it is the enhancement. No `SessionView` field, so no fixture change.
- **"The device's scope in the header."** No endpoint returns it after
  pairing; `/info` is unauthenticated (`src/app.rs:3568`), and the envelope
  carries only `epoch` and `revision` (`:3730`). §5's "the host answers
  with the device's scope" is not true of the code. The plan adds an
  authenticated `GET /api/v1/device`. It is also the page's cheap probe for
  "am I still paired".
- **"'Revoked' said plainly."** `authenticate` (`src/app.rs:3125-3153`)
  refuses a revoked token and a never-valid one with the same code,
  `unauthorized`. No new code: the page keeps a non-secret marker of what
  it paired with (below), so a 401 while it holds a token is "revoked or
  forgotten", and a changed `/info` key is "identity changed".
- **"Any path outside `/api/v1/` is refused."** True, but on the frame,
  after the request was queued (`src/app.rs:3023`). The static paths are
  answered on the connection thread before the queue, because they need no
  core state (§4.1: "the frame does core state only").
- **§5's "a relayed request through a substituted certificate fails".**
  Not true for a browser: the page is what posts `spki_sha256` to `/pair`,
  so under a relay the impostor's page supplies the host's real key. The
  `key` in the URL catches a genuine page on the wrong genuine host (a
  second installation at that address, a rotated key), not an impostor.
  §5 says so in the amendment.
- **Facts, Unresolved 8: "the code is single-use, refused after its first
  attempt."** The tree says otherwise. The code closes with the first
  *successful* `/pair` (`src/core/remote.rs:65-70`) and a wrong code counts
  toward three (`:56-64`). So a leaked URL is usable until the owner's own
  pairing succeeds or five minutes pass. That is the exposure the QR has
  today; the page sends the code once and the window closes on success, so
  a URL read from history after the pairing is dead. The plan does not
  change the window.
- **Facts, Unresolved 7: "whether `KeyPair::from_pem` exists for a reissue
  is unverified."** It is already called at `src/adapters/remote.rs:137`
  and `:146`; reissuing over the stored key compiles.
- **Decision 1's click-through.** The facts settle that on iOS a
  click-through does not carry `wss://` (WebKit 41419; code-server's iPad
  guide), and Unresolved 1 leaves open whether iOS offers one at all. The
  plan therefore does not make the socket, or the page, depend on it (see
  Decision 1).

## The record

No new record kind, no `model.rs` change, no `SCHEMA_VERSION` (16,
`src/core/model.rs:12`) or `VIEWS_SCHEMA_VERSION` (7, `:612`) bump. A
browser is a `PairedDevice` (`src/ports/remote.rs:96-107`) in
`devices.json`, which is an unversioned bare list; the name is the page's
`device_name` (`remote_pair`, `src/app.rs:3650`), cut to 64 characters by
`new_device` (`src/core/remote.rs:166-175`). **Decision 6: the name is
enough**, no `kind` field (the dialog lists it like any device and
Revoke works unchanged). Rehydration is unchanged: `IdentityLoaded`
(`src/core/remote.rs:22-30`) puts the devices back, `authenticate` checks
the token hash on every request.

One change to `identity.json`: the certificate gains names and a bounded
validity (Decision 1), and the file records which, so a reissue happens
when they change and not on every launch (a reissue changes the
certificate, and a browser's exception is per certificate).

- `Identity` (`src/ports/remote.rs:26-42`) gains
  `#[serde(default)] certificate_names: Vec<String>` and
  `#[serde(default)] certificate_not_after: Option<SystemTime>`.
- `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION` (1 today, `src/ports/remote.rs:17`) goes to
  **the value there at implementation time, plus one**; a ticket landing in
  parallel may take the next number first. Readers accept the older file
  (both fields default); an identity with no `certificate_not_after` is
  reissued once at the next launch. There is no migration step to write
  beyond the defaults: `RemoteFiles::load` is plain serde
  (`src/adapters/remote.rs:49`). `Identity` is built literally in
  `src/adapters/remote.rs:117`, `src/core/tests.rs:11769` and
  `tests/ui.rs:7436`; those three gain the fields.
- The SPKI does not move (same key), so every pin and every pairing holds.
  `make_identity` today sets no subjectAltName and no validity
  (`src/adapters/remote.rs:95-127`); the "year 4096" comment at `:91` is
  unverified (Facts, Unresolved 7). The new certificate sets explicitly:
  SANs, `serverAuth` EKU, `not_before` a day back, `not_after` 800 days out
  (iOS 825-day ceiling, Facts Settled), `IsCa::NoCa`.

**The page's own state on the device** (not a host record): in
`localStorage`, `sb.<server_id>` = `{token, device_id, name, scope, key,
host_name}`. See Decision 2 for why the token is there.

## The signals

None new. There is no `changed` kind or event type to add: the page
consumes the existing `hello`, `changed {session|sessions|waiting|
conversation|screen}`, `removed`, `watching` and `resync_required`
(`docs/remote-client.md` §4.4) and the revision rule. `GET /api/v1/device`
is a read, not a signal; the page refetches it on `hello` and every 30 s.

The page's live/poll behaviour is a client rule, specified in the UI
section because it follows from a settled fact: a click-through may not
carry `wss://` (iOS), so the page must work with no socket.

## The actions and effects

No `AppAction` or `Effect` variant: nothing here changes core state. The
pairing window, `OpenPairing`/`Paired`/`PairingFailed` and the devices are
as they are. What is added lives at the edges.

### Decisions settled here

**1. Trust: the click-through is the trust step; the certificate download
is offered beside it, not required.** The default must work whichever way
O1 and Unresolved 1 are answered, so:
- *Default.* Page and REST over HTTPS after whatever the browser lets the
  owner do (a click-through where one exists). The pairing dialog says in a
  sentence: "The first visit shows a certificate warning. Continue past it;
  the page then checks this host's key against the one in the link. That
  check catches the wrong Switchboard, not a stranger on your network
  serving a copy of this page: pair only from this dialog's code, on your
  own network." This is what the click-through buys: transport encryption
  to whoever answered, and the page's key comparison. It does not buy
  authentication of the host (a browser cannot read the certificate it is
  talking over, so the `/info` comparison proves only what the host
  *claims*; notes l.217-227).
- *The socket is optional.* The page opens `wss://` and, if it has not
  seen `hello` in 5 s or the socket closes, runs **polling mode**:
  `GET waiting`, the open project's sessions and the open session's
  content every 5 s, retrying the socket every 60 s. The header says
  "live" or "polling". The acceptance step "a session that starts waiting
  moves to the top without a reload" holds in both modes (within 5 s when
  polling). The socket is never a precondition of the page.
- *Enhancement, behind the default.* `GET /switchboard.crt` serves the
  certificate (DER, `application/x-x509-ca-cert`), and the landing screen
  links it as "Trust this host's certificate" for a device whose browser
  refuses the socket. The certificate is public (every TLS handshake sends
  it), so serving it before pairing reveals nothing. Whether iOS then
  accepts `wss://` with this certificate (it may need `CA:true`, per the
  code-server guide; Facts O1) is the owner's to confirm on a device; the
  plan does not claim it works and the README says "untested on a device".
- *Names.* The certificate carries SANs `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, the
  address from `local_address()` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:962`) and
  `<hostname -s>.local`, because Chrome and Safari match names only
  against SANs (Facts, Settled) and iOS requires one. `.local` reaches
  Mobile Safari over mDNS (Facts, Settled; not tested on a device), but
  the URL in the QR uses the IP, which needs no resolver. The certificate
  is reissued over the stored key (`KeyPair::from_pem`) in
  `load_identity` (`src/app.rs:2782`) when `certificate_names` differs from
  the current names or `certificate_not_after` is under 30 days away; never
  in `bind_remote`, which would loop through `Effect::SaveIdentity`. An
  address that moves while the app runs is covered at the next launch
  (the `.local` name covers the common case); the dialog's text says so.

**2. The token: `localStorage`, sent as `Authorization: Bearer` on `fetch`
and as a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` value on the socket. No cookie.**
Why: cookies are not isolated by port (RFC 6265 §8.5, Facts Settled), so a
cookie would go to every HTTPS service on the Mac; a `Strict` cookie can be
missing from a WebSocket in a restored Safari tab (WebKit 200345 and
232666, Facts Settled); and `Secure` on an IP host is unanswered (Facts,
Unresolved 5). The protocol route depends on none of these (Unresolved 4).
Cost, said in the dialog's sentence and the spec: any script on the origin
can read `localStorage`. The origin serves only our two files, under a CSP
with `script-src 'self'` and no inline script, and the page writes every
untrusted string (session names, replies, screens) with `textContent`,
never `innerHTML`; a test asserts the latter. The token is never in a URL
(§5).
- The socket offers two protocols, `switchboard.v1` and the token
  (base64url is a legal `token`, Facts Settled). The host takes the second
  value as the bearer and **echoes `switchboard.v1` in the 101**, never the
  token: a browser fails a socket that offered protocols and got none
  (WHATWG step 11.2, Facts Settled). Native clients keep the header.
- *Origin.* RFC 6455 §4.2.2 says a server that does not validate `Origin`
  accepts connections from anywhere (Facts, Settled). `remote_subscribe`
  (`src/app.rs:2723`) refuses with 403 `bad_origin` when an `Origin` header
  is present and its authority is not the request's `Host`. Same-origin
  works whatever name the device used (IP, `.local`, loopback); no
  `Origin` (native clients) is accepted. Commands carry the bearer header,
  which a cross-site page cannot set, so POSTs need no check.
- *Op ids.* `crypto.randomUUID` is secure-context only (Facts, Settled) and
  whether a click-through origin is one is unanswered (Unresolved 2, O2).
  The page uses `getRandomValues` to make a UUID always; no branch.

**3. One QR, a URL.** The QR and "Copy invite" carry
`https://<host>:<port>/?code=<code>&key=<spki_sha256>&id=<server_id>` (an
IPv6 host in brackets). Nothing produces the JSON after this. The Swift
`PairingInvite.parse` (`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:
93-116`) tries a URL first (`URLComponents`: `code`, `key`, `id`, host and
port become `addresses`) and decodes the JSON second, so a pasted old
invite still works; the visionOS paste field, `ConnectionManager` and
`switchboard-remote pair` all go through `parse` and need no change. That
is the four `Sources` users and eight `Tests` files of Facts, Settled; none
reads `addresses` as more than a list.

**4. Static paths.** Answered by the connection thread in `connection`
(`src/adapters/remote.rs:~773`), for `GET` only, before the rate check and
the frame; any other method on these paths goes to the frame and is
refused as today.

| Path | Content-Type | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `/` | `text/html; charset=utf-8` | `web/index.html` |
| `/app.js` | `text/javascript; charset=utf-8` | `web/app.js` |
| `/app.css` | `text/css; charset=utf-8` | `web/app.css` |
| `/favicon.ico` | none, `204` | (so the browser's guess costs no pool slot twice) |
| `/switchboard.crt` | `application/x-x509-ca-cert` | the identity's DER |

Every static reply carries `Cache-Control: no-store` (the page and the
host move together; nothing to revalidate), `X-Content-Type-Options:
nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` (the page's first URL carries
the code), `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; script-src 'self';
style-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; img-src 'self'; base-uri 'none';
form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'`, and **`Connection: close`**.
`connect-src 'self'` may not cover `wss:` on an older Safari; then the
socket is blocked and polling mode runs, which is the default design
working. The query on `/` is ignored by the server; it is never logged
(the connection thread logs nothing; `refuse`, `src/app.rs:3754`, never
logs a query either).
- *Pool and rate.* §4.1 allows four unauthenticated connections and the
  accept loop drops a fifth (`src/adapters/remote.rs:699-706`). A static GET
  with `Connection: close` frees its slot when the reply is written, so a
  page load (three files, up to three parallel connections, plus the
  favicon) holds the pool only for the length of the transfer; a browser's
  kept-alive connection never sits in it for 30 s. They count against the
  same unauthenticated pool as everything before pairing. They get a rate
  window of their own, `STATIC_PER_MINUTE = 120` beside `PAIR_PER_MINUTE` and
  `INFO_PER_MINUTE` (`:583-587`), answered 429 past it. How many parallel
  connections iOS Safari opens, and whether a page load plus the warning's
  failed handshake exhausts the pool, is O5 and Unresolved 6: the plan
  builds to a small count (the page is three files, no fonts, no images)
  and the owner measures before the pool size is touched. If a connection
  is dropped at accept, the page's `fetch` retries once after 1 s.
- *Without a code and without a token* the landing screen shows the host
  name and the short key from `/info`, the sentence "Open Remote devices on
  the Mac, choose Allow pairing, and scan the code", a code field (the key
  is taken from `/info`; the owner compares its short form with the
  dialog's) and the certificate link.
- `RemoteRequest` and `RemoteReply` are in `src/adapters/remote.rs:359-393`,
  not under `ports/`. No test builds either as a literal; `RemoteReply` is
  built in `src/adapters/remote.rs:506` and `src/app.rs` at `:1664`,
  `:1679`, `:2365`, `:2371`, `:2376`, `:3570` and in the helpers (Facts,
  Settled). So `RemoteReply` is left alone (static replies never reach
  the frame). `RemoteRequest` gains `host: Option<String>`,
  `origin: Option<String>` and `subprotocol: Option<String>` (the offered
  list, token excluded). `read_request` (`:444-513`) reads `host`,
  `origin` and `sec-websocket-protocol`; on an upgrade with no
  `Authorization` it sets `bearer` from the protocol list's non-

### Decisions settled here

is offered beside it, not required.** The default must work whichever way
O1 and Unresolved 1 are answered, so:

  owner do (a click-through where one exists). The pairing dialog says in a
  sentence: "The first visit shows a certificate warning. Continue past it;
  the page then checks this host's key against the one in the link. That
  check catches the wrong Switchboard, not a stranger on your network
  serving a copy of this page: pair only from this dialog's code, on your
  own network." This is what the click-through buys: transport encryption
  to whoever answered, and the page's key comparison. It does not buy
  authentication of the host (a browser cannot read the certificate it is
  talking over, so the `/info` comparison proves only what the host
  *claims*; notes l.217-227).
- *The socket is optional.* The page opens `wss://` and, if it has not
  seen `hello` in 5 s or the socket closes, runs **polling mode**:
  `GET waiting`, the open project's sessions and the open session's
  content every 5 s, retrying the socket every 60 s. The header says
  "live" or "polling". The acceptance step "a session that starts waiting
  moves to the top without a reload" holds in both modes (within 5 s when
  polling). The socket is never a precondition of the page.
- *Enhancement, behind the default.* `GET /switchboard.crt` serves the
  certificate (DER, `application/x-x509-ca-cert`), and the landing screen
  links it as "Trust this host's certificate" for a device whose browser
  refuses the socket. The certificate is public (every TLS handshake sends
  it), so serving it before pairing reveals nothing. Whether iOS then
  accepts `wss://` with this certificate (it may need `CA:true`, per the
  code-server guide; Facts O1) is the owner's to confirm on a device; the
  plan does not claim it works and the README says "untested on a device".

  address from `local_address()` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:962`) and
  `<hostname -s>.local`, because Chrome and Safari match names only
  against SANs (Facts, Settled) and iOS requires one. `.local` reaches

  the URL in the QR uses the IP, which needs no resolver. The certificate
  is reissued over the stored key (`KeyPair::from_pem`) in

  the current names or `certificate_not_after` is under 30 days away; never
  in `bind_remote`, which would loop through `Effect::SaveIdentity`. An
  address that moves while the app runs is covered at the next launch
  (the `.local` name covers the common case); the dialog's text says so.

and as a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` value on the socket. No cookie.**

cookie would go to every HTTPS service on the Mac; a `Strict` cookie can be
missing from a WebSocket in a restored Safari tab (WebKit 200345 and
232666, Facts Settled); and `Secure` on an IP host is unanswered (Facts,

can read `localStorage`. The origin serves only our two files, under a CSP
with `script-src 'self'` and no inline script, and the page writes every
untrusted string (session names, replies, screens) with `textContent`,
never `innerHTML`; a test asserts the latter. The token is never in a URL
(§5).

  value as the bearer and **echoes `switchboard.v1` in the 101**, never the
  token: a browser fails a socket that offered protocols and got none
  (WHATWG step 11.2, Facts Settled). Native clients keep the header.

  accepts connections from anywhere (Facts, Settled). `remote_subscribe`

  is present and its authority is not the request's `Host`. Same-origin
  works whatever name the device used (IP, `.local`, loopback); no
  `Origin` (native clients) is accepted. Commands carry the bearer header,
  which a cross-site page cannot set, so POSTs need no check.
- *Op ids.* `crypto.randomUUID` is secure-context only (Facts, Settled) and
  whether a click-through origin is one is unanswered (Unresolved 2, O2).
  The page uses `getRandomValues` to make a UUID always; no branch.

`https://<host>:<port>/?code=<code>&key=<spki_sha256>&id=<server_id>` (an
IPv6 host in brackets). Nothing produces the JSON after this. The Swift

93-116`) tries a URL first (`URLComponents`: `code`, `key`, `id`, host and
port become `addresses`) and decodes the JSON second, so a pasted old
invite still works; the visionOS paste field, `ConnectionManager` and
`switchboard-remote pair` all go through `parse` and need no change. That
is the four `Sources` users and eight `Tests` files of Facts, Settled; none
reads `addresses` as more than a list.

(`src/adapters/remote.rs:~773`), for `GET` only, before the rate check and
